newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: BRITAIN CONSIDERS FUNDING ZIMBABWE LAND REFORMS.
newsitem.headline: BRITAIN CONSIDERS FUNDING ZIMBABWE LAND REFORMS.

text.p: The British government said on Thursday it was considering funding a new land resettlement programme in Zimbabwe after years of withholding aid over the use of a controversial land acquisition policy.

Mark Lowcock, the head of a five-member British land appraisal mission to Zimbabwe, told a news conference London was talking to President Robert Mugabe's government about a resettlement scheme aimed at reducing rural poverty in the southern African state.

"We envisage a programme, including land acquisition, which the British government could help fund on the basis of the willing-seller principle," said Lowcock, who is deputy head of the Overseas Development Agency's office in Harare.

He said it was still too early to say what the outcome would be, "but on the basis of our work so far, we are confident it should be possible to design a further programme which will justify funding by the British government and other interested donors."

Britain -- Zimbabwe's former colonial master -- helped settle thousands of black peasants after Zimbabwe's 1980 independence, but it withheld some money in the late 1980s when Mugabe adopted a controversial policy of forcibly acquiring farms from minority whites who occupy most of the country's fertile land.

Mugabe, who swept to power in 1980 after a seven-year guerrilla war during on a promise to give blacks a bigger share of the land, has forcibly bought some farms under that policy, but he has avoided the wholesale seizures many economists feared would derail Zimbabwe's mainstay agriculture sector.
Over the past two years, Mugabe has been threatening to nationalise the white-owned farms without paying any compensation if Britain does not provide some money.
At least a quarter of Zimbabwe's 10.5 million people has applied to be resettled.

Lowcock, whose two-week land appraisal mission to Zimbabwe is due to end on October 4, said he did not know how much Britain was prepared to spend on a new resettlement scheme, but he said it would not be restricted to the Z$56 million (U.S.$5.42 million) left from the old allocation of Z$323 million (U.S.$31.2 million).

"The principle objective of the (new resettlement) programme would be reduction of rural poverty. The programme would need to have an acceptable economic rate of return, be cost effective and be sustainable," he said.
The scale and pace of implementation, Lowcock said, would need to reflect the implementation capacity and other constraints faced by relevant government and other institutions in Zimbabwe.
